theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A supplier offers 8% off a J$25,000,000 contract if the agency commits to three years instead of two. What is the saving on the J$25,000,000?

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: You will lead final negotiations with the preferred bidder for a five-year contract to supply and maintain ambulances for a public health authority. Describe how you would plan the negotiation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first confirm what the procurement rules and the tender documents allow us to negotiate, so that we do not change the basis on which other bidders competed. I would gather evidence: the evaluation report, the bidder's offer, our budget, market information on vehicle prices and parts, and the performance records of any current supplier. I would calculate the total cost of ownership over five years, including servicing, parts, tyres, downtime and resale value, and prepare a should-cost estimate. Then the team would set objectives in order of priority: for example, a guaranteed response time for repairs and a replacement vehicle during breakdowns as musts, a lower price as a want, and staged deliveries as something we could give. We would set our opening position, target and walk-away point, and note our best alternative, such as the second-ranked bidder if the rules allow. I would form a team with a procurement lead, a fleet expert, a finance officer, a legal adviser and a note-taker, confirm everyone's authority and have each sign a conflict of interest declaration. Finally, I would agree an agenda with the bidder and rehearse the main issues.
markingPoints: Confirms what the rules and documents allow
Gathers evidence and calculates total cost of ownership
Sets prioritised objectives and possible concessions
Sets opening, target and walk-away positions and the alternative
Forms a team with roles, authority, declarations and an agenda

essays.stem: Explain how a supply positioning (Kraljic) matrix helps a public body decide its procurement and negotiation approach, giving an example for each of its four categories.
essays.modelAnswer: The matrix places each purchase according to its cost or impact on the organisation and the risk in its supply, such as few suppliers or long lead times. This shows where to spend negotiating effort. Routine items, such as stationery, have low impact and low risk: the body should simplify buying, for example through framework agreements, and spend little time negotiating. Leverage items, such as fuel or office paper bought in large amounts from many suppliers, have high impact but low risk: the body can use competition and volume to drive down price and improve terms. Bottleneck items, such as a spare part available from only one firm, have low cost but high risk: the aim is to secure supply, for example by holding stock, agreeing guaranteed delivery times or finding alternatives, rather than pressing hard on price. Strategic items, such as a hospital's imaging equipment and maintenance, have high impact and high risk: these need careful planning, a skilled team, attention to total cost and service levels, and a long-term relationship with the supplier. Using the matrix helps the body match its negotiating approach to each purchase.
markingPoints: Explains the two dimensions: impact or cost, and supply risk
Describes routine items with an example and approach
Describes leverage items with an example and approach
Describes bottleneck items with an example and approach
Describes strategic items with an example and approach

essays.stem: A ministry needs 4 standby generators. Supplier A charges J$5,800,000 each, with servicing of J$250,000 and fuel of J$900,000 per generator a year. Supplier B charges J$5,000,000 each, with servicing of J$400,000 and fuel of J$1,050,000 per generator a year. Over five years, compare the total cost of ownership for the 4 generators and explain how this should shape the negotiation.
essays.modelAnswer: For Supplier A, each generator costs J$250,000 + J$900,000 = J$1,150,000 a year to run, or J$5,750,000 over five years. Its total cost is J$5,800,000 + J$5,750,000 = J$11,550,000, so 4 generators cost J$46,200,000. For Supplier B, running costs are J$400,000 + J$1,050,000 = J$1,450,000 a year, or J$7,250,000 over five years. Its total is J$5,000,000 + J$7,250,000 = J$12,250,000, so 4 generators cost J$49,000,000. Checking: J$49,000,000 − J$46,200,000 = J$2,800,000, or J$700,000 per generator. Supplier A is cheaper over five years by J$2,800,000, even though its price is J$800,000 higher per generator. In the negotiation, the team should focus on total cost, not the purchase price alone. With Supplier A, it could seek a fixed servicing price for five years, a guarantee of the fuel use claimed, spare parts on hand and a warranty. With Supplier B, it would need large cuts in servicing or proof of lower fuel use. The team should also check the assumptions, such as fuel prices and hours run, before agreeing.
markingPoints: Calculates A's five-year cost: J$11,550,000 each, J$46,200,000 for four
Calculates B's five-year cost: J$12,250,000 each, J$49,000,000 for four
Identifies A as cheaper by J$2,800,000 despite the higher price, with a check
Uses total cost to set negotiation aims, such as fixed servicing and fuel guarantees
Checks the assumptions behind the figures

essays.stem: Explain how the procurement rules for public bodies, described by their general purpose, and the principles of probity limit and guide negotiation with suppliers.
essays.modelAnswer: The procurement rules for public bodies aim to get value for money while treating suppliers fairly, keeping the process open and competitive, and making officers accountable for public money. This shapes negotiation in several ways. Negotiation may happen only where the procurement method and tender documents allow it, usually with the preferred bidder after evaluation. It must not change the scope or terms so much that other bidders would have competed differently; if it would, the body should consider re-tendering. Other bidders' prices and information must be kept confidential and never used as a bargaining tool. Probity means acting with honesty, fairness and openness. Team members must declare any conflict of interest and step aside if one exists, refuse gifts and hospitality, and treat all suppliers equally. Negotiators must not make false claims, such as inventing a lower offer, and must not exceed their delegated authority. Every offer, concession and decision should be recorded, so that the process can be audited and explained to oversight bodies and the public. Within these limits, negotiators can still press firmly for better price, service and risk terms.
markingPoints: States the general aims of the rules: value for money, fairness, openness, competition, accountability
Explains when negotiation is allowed and the limit on changing the basis of competition
Keeps other bids confidential
Applies probity: declarations, no gifts, honesty, equal treatment, authority limits
Requires full records for audit, while still negotiating firmly

essays.stem: Describe how you would conduct the negotiation meeting itself, from the opening to the close, to reach a good agreement with a supplier.
essays.modelAnswer: I would open by welcoming the supplier's team, introducing our team and confirming the purpose, the agenda, the time available and who has authority to agree. I would set a positive, professional tone, because we want a working relationship after the deal. Next I would explore both sides' interests by asking open questions, for example why the supplier needs a deposit, and listening carefully, while our note-taker records what is said. I would then make or respond to offers, starting from our planned position and supporting it with evidence such as total cost figures and market prices. Concessions would be traded, not given away: "if you include training for our technicians, we can accept delivery in two batches." I would deal with one issue at a time but keep the whole package in view, and call a short break to consult the team when needed. If talks stalled, I would look for other options, such as different service levels. Before closing, I would summarise every agreed point and any open issues, confirm that both sides understand them the same way, and explain that the agreement is subject to approval and a written contract.
markingPoints: Opens with purpose, agenda, roles, authority and a professional tone
Explores interests with open questions and active listening, with notes
Makes offers backed by evidence
Trades concessions, uses breaks and handles deadlock
Summarises agreed points and states that approval and a written contract follow

essays.stem: A supplier's team uses three pressure tactics: a short deadline, a "take it or leave it" offer and an angry outburst. Explain how a public sector negotiator should respond to each.
essays.modelAnswer: With a short deadline, such as "this price ends at 5 p.m. today", the negotiator should not be rushed. She should say calmly that the agency must check the offer and get approval in line with its rules, ask why the deadline exists, and test whether it is real. A good offer will usually still be there tomorrow, and a rushed decision may break the rules or miss a problem. With a "take it or leave it" offer, she should not argue about the words but explore what lies behind them: ask what makes the offer final and look for other variables, such as delivery dates, payment terms or service levels. If the offer is still worse than the agency's walk-away point and its best alternative, she should be prepared to decline politely. With an angry outburst, she should stay calm and polite, not raise her voice or react personally, acknowledge the concern, and if necessary call a short break. Afterwards she can bring the discussion back to the issues and the facts. In every case she should keep to her authority, act honestly and record what happened.
markingPoints: Responds to the deadline by checking, seeking approval and testing it
Responds to take-it-or-leave-it by exploring interests and other variables
Is ready to walk away if the offer is below the walk-away point
Handles the outburst calmly, uses a break and refocuses on issues
Keeps within authority, acts honestly and records events

essays.stem: Evaluate the non-price terms a public body should negotiate in a strategic contract for hospital cleaning services, and explain why each matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Service levels matter most: clear, measurable standards for cleanliness in wards, theatres and toilets, response times for spills and how quality will be checked. Without them, the hospital cannot hold the contractor to account or protect patients from infection. Remedies should be agreed, such as deductions when standards are missed and the right to end the contract for repeated failure, so that poor service has a cost. Staffing terms, such as minimum staff on each shift, training in infection control and vetting of workers, protect patients and property. Health and safety terms should require the safe use, labelling and storage of chemicals and correct protective equipment, in line with safety law. Price adjustment terms, linked to a published index or to changes in the minimum wage, manage cost changes fairly over several years. Payment terms should link payment to monthly performance reports. Reporting and review meetings keep both sides working on problems. Exit and handover terms make sure the service continues if the contract ends. Each of these may be worth more to the hospital than a small cut in price, because they protect quality and reduce risk.
markingPoints: Service levels with measures and checks, and why they matter
Remedies for poor performance
Staffing, training, vetting and safety terms
Price adjustment and payment terms linked to performance
Reporting, review and exit terms, weighed against price

essays.stem: An agency's budget for three-year ICT support is J$80,000,000, but the preferred bidder's price is J$86,400,000. The bidder offers: (a) a 5% price cut if weekend on-site support is replaced by remote support; and (b) a further J$1,800,000 off if the agency pays within 15 days instead of 30. Analyse the offers and recommend what the team should do.
essays.modelAnswer: The bid is J$86,400,000 − J$80,000,000 = J$6,400,000 over budget, which is 8% of the budget. Offer (a) cuts 5% of J$86,400,000, which is J$4,320,000, giving J$82,080,000. Adding offer (b) takes off J$1,800,000 more, giving J$80,280,000. Checking: J$86,400,000 − J$4,320,000 − J$1,800,000 = J$80,280,000. Even with both offers, the price is still J$280,000 over budget. Before accepting (a), the team should check with the ICT unit whether remote weekend support is enough for its systems, for example by looking at how often weekend faults needed someone on site; if critical systems need on-site help, the saving could be a false economy. Before accepting (b), the finance unit must confirm that the payment system can reliably pay in 15 days, or the agency would fail its promise. I would recommend negotiating further: accept (a) only with a guaranteed on-site response for critical faults, accept (b) if finance confirms it, and ask the bidder to close the last J$280,000 gap, for example through training or a small scope change the rules allow. If the gap remains, the team should seek approval from the authorised officer rather than agree beyond its limit.
markingPoints: Calculates the J$6,400,000 (8%) overrun
Calculates J$82,080,000 after (a) and J$80,280,000 after (b), with a check
Tests whether remote weekend support is acceptable
Checks that the agency can pay within 15 days
Recommends further negotiation and seeks approval rather than exceeding authority

essays.stem: Explain how a public body should organise its team for a strategic procurement negotiation, including roles, authority limits and communication during the talks.
essays.modelAnswer: The team should be small enough to work well but cover the skills the deal needs. A lead negotiator, usually from procurement, speaks for the team and manages the meeting. A technical expert, such as an engineer or ICT specialist, judges whether offers meet the requirement. A finance officer checks prices, total cost and budget effects. A legal or contracts adviser checks the wording of terms. A note-taker records every offer, concession and agreement. Before the talks, the team should agree its plan and confirm in writing what authority the lead has, for example the highest price and the concessions she may agree; anything beyond that must go back to the officer with delegated authority. Every member should sign a conflict of interest and confidentiality declaration. During the talks, the team should speak with one voice: only the lead makes or accepts offers, while others answer questions when invited. The team should agree simple signals, such as passing a note or asking for a short break, so that members can raise concerns privately. After each session, the team should meet to review progress and agree the next steps.
markingPoints: Names suitable roles: lead, technical, finance, legal, note-taker
Confirms the lead's authority in writing and refers anything beyond it upward
Requires conflict of interest and confidentiality declarations
Speaks with one voice, with private signals and breaks
Reviews progress after each session

essays.stem: Explain what should happen after agreement is reached in a strategic procurement negotiation, up to the start of the contract and beyond, including records, approvals, debriefing and managing the supplier relationship.
essays.modelAnswer: Straight after the talks, the note-taker and the lead should write up the agreed points and send them to the supplier to confirm, so there is no misunderstanding. The full record of the negotiation, including offers and concessions, should be filed with the procurement file. The legal adviser should turn the agreed terms into the contract, and the finance officer should confirm that money is available. The contract and a short report explaining the outcome, the savings and any changes from the tender should then go to the officer or committee with the authority to approve it, in line with the procurement rules. Once approved, it is signed and, where the rules require, the award is published and unsuccessful bidders are told. The team should hold a debrief to record what went well and what to improve. A contract manager should then be named, with a plan for start-up, regular performance reviews against the service levels, and checks on payments. For a strategic supplier, the relationship should be managed actively, with regular meetings to solve problems, manage risks and look for improvements, and with records kept for audit.
markingPoints: Writes up and confirms the agreed points, and files the record
Prepares the contract and confirms funds
Gets approval from the authorised officer and handles award notices
Holds a debrief to capture lessons
Names a contract manager and manages performance and the relationship

practical1.title: Plan a strategic procurement negotiation
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a negotiation pack from a made-up public body (for example a municipal corporation's three-year fleet maintenance contract, a hospital's cleaning contract or a ministry's ICT support contract). It contains a summary of the tender evaluation and the preferred bidder's offer (above the budget), the budget, the bidder's past performance, market information, the parts of the tender documents that say what may be negotiated, and a cost sheet. As a group, prepare a negotiation plan pack containing: a one-page analysis of the purchase on a supply positioning (Kraljic) matrix and the supplier's bargaining power; a total cost of ownership calculation for the offer, with every sum checked twice; prioritised objectives (must, want and could give), with the opening position, target and walk-away point and the best alternative; a list of variables and concessions to trade; the team's roles and authority limits; a probity checklist with signed conflict of interest declarations (on a Centre form); and an agenda for the meeting. Give each member a named role: lead negotiator (keeps time, agrees the objectives and assembles the pack), cost analyst (prepares the total cost and should-cost figures), market analyst (prepares the matrix and bargaining power analysis), probity and rules officer (checks what may be negotiated and prepares the probity checklist), and agenda and records officer (prepares the agenda and the note-taking sheet). In a group of four, the lead negotiator also prepares the agenda. At the end, each member explains their part to the assessor in two minutes.
materials: Negotiation pack and cost sheet from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
Centre conflict of interest declaration forms
photos: The flipchart with roles, timetable and what the rules allow to be negotiated
The supply positioning matrix and bargaining power analysis
The total cost of ownership calculation with the second check marked
The objectives with opening, target and walk-away positions
The variables and concessions list and the signed declarations (names covered if preferred)
The agenda and the assembled plan pack
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the pack
Purchase is placed correctly on the matrix and supplier power is judged sensibly
Total cost figures are correct and were checked twice
Objectives are prioritised and the walk-away point fits the budget and the alternative
Plan negotiates only what the tender documents and rules allow
Concessions are planned to be traded, not given away
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up public body, bidder and figures; keep the pack confidential to the group and assessor
Do not use real firms' names or prices
Listen to every member's ideas respectfully and share the work fairly
Take short breaks and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Conduct a procurement negotiation role play and record the agreement
practical2.brief: Using a negotiation pack from the assessor (or the plan from Practical 1, if the assessor agrees), your group is the public body's negotiating team. The assessor and one or two other trainees play the preferred bidder's team, using role cards that include at least one pressure tactic. Hold a 30-minute negotiation meeting: open with the agenda and roles, explore interests, make and trade offers, handle the pressure tactic calmly, and close by summarising every agreed point and any open issues. After the meeting: (1) work out the final contract value, the saving or overrun against the budget and the five-year total cost, checking every sum twice; (2) write a one-page record of the agreed terms; (3) write a one-page approval memo to the officer with delegated authority, explaining the outcome and any point beyond the team's authority; (4) hold a 10-minute debrief and write three lessons learned. Give each member a named role: lead negotiator (opens, leads and closes the meeting), technical adviser (answers on service and specification), finance officer (checks offers during the meeting and works the final figures), note-taker (records every offer, concession and agreement), and probity and approvals officer (watches that the team stays within the rules and its authority, and drafts the approval memo). In a group of four, the finance officer also drafts the approval memo. Every member must speak in the meeting or the debrief.
materials: Negotiation pack and role cards from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Note-taking sheet, record of agreement and memo templates (optional)
photos: The meeting room set up with the agenda displayed
The negotiation in progress (table and notes only if anyone prefers no face)
The note-taker's record of offers and concessions
The final figures with the second check marked
The record of agreed terms and the approval memo
The debrief notes with three lessons learned
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Team opened clearly, explored interests and traded concessions rather than giving them away
Handled the pressure tactic calmly and did not agree beyond its authority
Kept other bidders' information confidential and acted honestly throughout
Final figures are correct and were checked twice
Record of agreement matches the notes, and the memo explains the outcome and any approval needed
safety: Treat the pack and role cards as confidential and use only the made-up names and figures
In the role play, stay respectful even when a role card is hostile; stop and take a break if anyone becomes upset
Ask permission before photographing anyone; photograph notes and the table if a person prefers
Share the workload fairly and take a short break between the meeting and the write-up
